name: Bon Scott
milestone_by_age_26: Co-led the Valentines, whose single 'My Old Man's a Groovy Old Man' reached #22 on the Australian chart in 1969 and 'Juliette' reached #28 in 1970, before joining Fraternity and releasing the album Livestock in 1971.
early_history_summary: Born in Scotland, Scott migrated to Australia at age 6 and grew up in working-class Fremantle. He began drumming in a community pipe band as a child, formed his first band the Spektors in 1964 at age 18, and co-founded the Valentines in 1966, becoming one of Perth's leading pop groups before moving to Melbourne in 1967.
family_context_summary: Born to Charles Belford Scott, a baker, and Isabelle Mitchell in Forfar, Scotland; the family migrated to Australia in 1952 and settled in working-class Fremantle.
primary_early_advantage_tags: working-class background, juvenile institution, migration, 1960s rock boom, Australian music scene
evidence_summary: Bon Scott grew up in a working-class Scottish migrant family in Fremantle, Australia, with no documented family connection to professional music. He left school at 15, spent time in a juvenile institution, and began performing in bands from age 18, building years of live performance experience before achieving chart success. The 1960s Australian pop-rock boom provided a structural wave, and his co-leadership with Vince Lovegrove in the Valentines gave him a complementary creative partnership. His path was driven by early immersion in performance and persistence through adversity rather than inherited advantages.

name: Jacques Dubochet
milestone_by_age_26: Received physics engineering diploma in 1967 at age 25, but Nobel Prize-winning cryo-electron microscopy work came in the early 1980s at age ~40; no material independently verifiable milestone by age 26.
family_context_summary: Born in Aigle, Switzerland; parents noticed his dyslexia and advocated for his education, sending him to boarding school in German-speaking Switzerland.

name: Pelé
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1958 FIFA World Cup with Brazil at age 17, scoring a hat-trick in the semifinal against France and two goals in the final against Sweden, becoming the youngest World Cup winner and scorer in history.
early_history_summary: Pelé grew up in poverty in Bauru, São Paulo, taught to play football by his father Dondinho, a former professional footballer. He could not afford a proper ball and played with a grapefruit or sock stuffed with newspaper, shining shoes to help his family. Former Brazil international Waldemar de Brito discovered him and arranged a trial at Santos FC in 1956, where he debuted at 15 and became the league's top scorer at 16.
family_context_summary: Born in Três Corações to Dondinho (João Ramos do Nascimento), a professional footballer of modest means whose career was cut short by injury, and Celeste Arantes; grew up in deep poverty in Bauru.
parent_family_domain_summary: Pelé's father Dondinho was a professional footballer who directly taught him the game and instilled a passion for football from early childhood; his uncle was also a professional player.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father footballer, poverty, prodigy, Waldemar de Brito mentor, Santos FC pipeline
evidence_summary: Pelé was born into deep poverty in Brazil to a father who was a professional footballer whose career was derailed by injury, providing direct domain knowledge and training from childhood. He could not afford a proper ball and shined shoes to survive, but former Brazil international Waldemar de Brito recognized his extraordinary talent and arranged a trial at Santos FC, one of Brazil's top clubs. By 15 he debuted professionally, by 16 he was the league's top scorer, and at 17 he won the World Cup. His path combined a prodigy-level physical talent, a father's domain knowledge, a key mentor's advocacy, and an elite club pipeline, all catalyzed by the adversity of extreme poverty.

name: Aleksandr Karelin
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold in Greco-Roman super-heavyweight wrestling at the 1988 Seoul Olympics at age 21, having become world junior champion in 1987 and earned a place on the Soviet national team.
early_history_summary: Karelin was born in Novosibirsk, Siberia, weighing 15 pounds at birth. He began wrestling at age 13 in 1981 under coach Viktor Kuznetsov at the Novosibirsk Electrotechnical Institute, after trying boxing, skiing, and other sports. He quickly achieved success in Soviet junior tournaments, winning world junior championships in 1985 and 1987, and made the Soviet national team in 1986.
family_context_summary: Born in Novosibirsk to a truck driver father who was an amateur boxer and an office worker mother; described as a descendant of intellectuals forcibly relocated to Siberia; working-class family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Karelin's father was an amateur boxer who encouraged physical strength and directed him toward combat sports, though not wrestling specifically.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, Kuznetsov coach, physical prodigy, Siberian hardship, amateur boxer father
evidence_summary: Karelin was born an extraordinary physical specimen (15 pounds at birth) to a working-class family in Novosibirsk, Siberia, with a father who was an amateur boxer and encouraged strength. He began wrestling relatively late at 13 but was guided by Viktor Kuznetsov, who remained his only coach throughout his entire career, providing sustained individualized training. The Soviet sports pipeline, including the Burevestnik sports society and a military sports company, concentrated opportunity and resources. His legendary training intensity, including running through thigh-deep snow and rowing boats, combined with his natural physical dominance to produce an Olympic gold at 21.

name: Tupac Shakur
milestone_by_age_26: Released debut solo album 2Pacalypse Now on Interscope Records in November 1991 at age 20, establishing him as a central figure in West Coast hip-hop with politically conscious lyrics.
early_history_summary: Born in New York City to Black Panther Party members, Tupac relocated to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1988 at age 17. He began recording as MC New York, attended poetry classes with Leila Steinberg who became his first manager, and was signed by Atron Gregory, manager of Digital Underground. He worked as a roadie and backup dancer for Digital Underground before landing his own Interscope deal and releasing 2Pacalypse Now in 1991.
family_context_summary: Born to Afeni Shakur (born Alice Faye Williams), a Black Panther Party activist, and Billy Garland, also a Black Panther; raised in poverty by his single mother who struggled with crack cocaine addiction; family moved frequently between New York, Baltimore, and California.
parent_family_domain_summary: Tupac's mother Afeni Shakur was a Black Panther Party member whose political activism and revolutionary worldview deeply shaped his lyrical content and social consciousness; his stepfather Mutulu Shakur was also a political activist.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Black Panther heritage, poverty, Bay Area hip-hop, Leila Steinberg mentor, Digital Underground crew, political consciousness
evidence_summary: Tupac Shakur was born into extreme adversity: his mother was a Black Panther activist who was pregnant with him while imprisoned, and he grew up in poverty with a mother battling drug addiction. His family's political radicalism gave him a distinctive lens on urban inequality that became the core of his lyrical voice. After moving to the Bay Area in 1988, he immersed himself in the exploding West Coast hip-hop scene, found a mentor in Leila Steinberg and a platform in Digital Underground, and leveraged the structural wave of early 1990s rap to release his debut album at 20. His path was defined by constraint-driven self-creation rather than inherited advantages.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
milestone_by_age_26: Wrote the unpublished Enquire program at CERN in 1980 at age 25, but the World Wide Web was invented in 1989 at age 34; no material independently verifiable milestone by age 26.
family_context_summary: Born in London to mathematicians and computer scientists Mary Lee Woods and Conway Berners-Lee, who both worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, the first commercially built computer.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were mathematicians and computer scientists who worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, providing deep early exposure to computing and information science.

name: Muhammad Ali
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic light heavyweight gold medal at the 1960 Rome Olympics at age 18, compiling a 100-8 amateur record including six Kentucky Golden Gloves and two national AAU titles, then turned professional in October 1960.
early_history_summary: Born Cassius Clay in segregated Louisville, Kentucky, Ali was introduced to boxing at age 12 when his stolen bicycle led him to police officer Joe Martin, a boxing trainer. He won his first bout within six weeks, then rose rapidly through amateur boxing, winning Golden Gloves titles and national championships before claiming Olympic gold at 18 and turning professional the same year.
family_context_summary: Born in segregated Louisville, Kentucky to Cassius Clay Sr., a sign painter, and Odessa Grady Clay, a household worker; the family was middle class by Black Louisville standards but lived in a modest two-bedroom house in the West End.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; Ali's father was a sign painter and musician with no documented boxing background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Joe Martin mentor, Golden Gloves pipeline, physical prodigy, racial segregation, Louisville
evidence_summary: Muhammad Ali grew up in segregated Louisville in a working-class Black family with no boxing heritage, discovered the sport by chance at 12 when his bicycle was stolen and he met police officer Joe Martin at a gym. Martin provided sustained training that turned a raw but extraordinarily athletic teenager into a national amateur champion within six years. Ali's exceptional speed and footwork for a heavyweight were evident early, producing a 100-8 amateur record and Olympic gold at 18. The adversity of growing up in the segregated South, including the murder of Emmett Till, fueled his urgency and distinctive voice. His path was defined by physical prodigy and a chance mentor encounter rather than inherited advantages.

name: Alexander Godunov
milestone_by_age_26: Joined the Bolshoi Ballet in 1971 at age 22 as its youngest premier danseur, was chosen by legendary prima ballerina Maya Plisetskaya as her partner, and won gold at the Moscow International Ballet Competition in 1973 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born on Sakhalin Island, Godunov moved to Riga as a child where his mother enrolled him in the Riga Choreography School at age 9 in 1958, in the same class as Mikhail Baryshnikov. He graduated in 1966, toured with Igor Moiseyev's Young Ballet company for three years, then joined the Bolshoi Ballet in 1971, quickly rising to premier danseur with lead roles in Swan Lake and Giselle.
family_context_summary: Born in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk to Boris Godunov and Lidia Nicholaevna Studentova; parents divorced when he was young and his mother raised him and his brother in Riga, Latvia; mother enrolled him in ballet at 9 to prevent him from becoming a hooligan.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no family connection to ballet documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet ballet pipeline, Riga school, Baryshnikov peer, Plisetskaya partner, Bolshoi
evidence_summary: Alexander Godunov was born on Sakhalin Island to a divorced family with no documented ballet heritage; his mother enrolled him in ballet at 9 to keep him off the streets. He was selected from 250 applicants for the Riga Choreography School, where he trained alongside Mikhail Baryshnikov, and continued at the Bolshoi Choreographic School under Sergei Koren. The Soviet ballet pipeline provided elite training facilities, master teachers, and a direct path to the Bolshoi Ballet, which he joined at 22 as its youngest principal. Maya Plisetskaya chose him as her partner, and he won gold at the Moscow International Ballet Competition at 24. His rise was driven by the elite Soviet ballet system and physical talent rather than family advantages.

name: Judit Polgár
milestone_by_age_26: Became the youngest chess Grandmaster in history at age 15 in 1991, breaking Bobby Fischer's 33-year-old record, after winning the boys' World Youth Chess Championship at ages 12 and 14 and Olympic gold with Hungary in 1988 at age 12.
early_history_summary: Judit Polgár was the youngest of three sisters raised in Budapest as part of a deliberate educational experiment by her father László Polgár, a psychologist who believed any child could be raised to be a genius through early intensive specialization. She was homeschooled with chess as the primary focus, studying 8 hours a day alongside her sisters, and began playing tournaments at age 9, winning her first international tournament at the New York Open.
family_context_summary: Daughter of László Polgár, a Hungarian psychologist and educational theorist, and Klara Polgár, a teacher; parents deliberately designed a homeschooling experiment to raise prodigies, choosing chess as the specialization field; family was of modest means but dedicated all resources to the children's chess education.
parent_family_domain_summary: Judit's father László Polgár was a psychologist who authored 'Bring Up Genius!' and designed the entire educational experiment around chess, homeschooling his daughters with 8 hours of daily chess study and hiring professional GM trainers including Pal Benko and Alexander Chernin.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father educational experiment, homeschooling, chess immersion, sister peers, GM trainers, Hungarian chess tradition
evidence_summary: Judit Polgár was the product of a deliberate educational experiment by her father László Polgár, a psychologist who believed geniuses are made not born and chose chess as the vehicle. She was homeschooled from birth with 8 hours of daily chess study, surrounded by her two older sisters who were also competitive chess players, creating an exceptional peer training environment. The family hired professional grandmaster trainers including Pal Benko and Alexander Chernin, and the home was filled with chess books and 30 boards pinned to the wall. By 5 she could beat her father, by 9 she won an international tournament, by 12 she won Olympic gold, and at 15 she became the youngest grandmaster ever. The communist regime's resistance to homeschooling added urgency. Her path was entirely shaped by her father's domain expertise and educational design.

name: Guillermo Vilas
milestone_by_age_26: Won the year-end Masters Grand Prix title in 1974 at age 22, defeating Björn Borg and Ilie Năstase, and finished in the year-end top ten for the first time, establishing himself as a major contender.
early_history_summary: Born in Buenos Aires and raised in Mar del Plata, Vilas began playing tennis at age 5 under the direction of his father, a prosperous lawyer who was president of the Club Náutico de Mar del Plata. He won his first club title at 12, was Argentina's number one by 18, and turned professional in 1968, reaching his first career finals in 1972 and winning his first title in Buenos Aires in 1973.
family_context_summary: Born to José Roque Vilas, a prosperous notary/lawyer who served as president of the Club Náutico de Mar del Plata, and María Isabel Vilas; upper-middle-class family that provided early access to tennis facilities and directed him to the sport at age 5.
parent_family_domain_summary: Vilas's father was president of the Club Náutico de Mar del Plata and directed him to tennis at age 5 to keep him from playing soccer in the streets, providing direct access to facilities and early coaching through the club.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father lawyer, Club Náutico access, early tennis, Locicero coach, Open Era, Argentine tennis
evidence_summary: Guillermo Vilas was born into an upper-middle-class Argentine family; his father was a prosperous notary who served as president of the Club Náutico de Mar del Plata, giving Vilas direct access to tennis facilities from age 5. His father directed him away from soccer and toward tennis, and his first coach Felipe Locicero was discovered through the club. The Open Era beginning in 1968 created a structural wave of professionalization that Vilas rode, and his legendary 8-hour practice sessions and iron-man stamina drove him to the year-end top ten by 22. His early advantages were primarily financial and facility access through his father's position, combined with intense concentration and early specialization.

name: Michael Levitt
milestone_by_age_26: Published first paper in Journal of Molecular Biology in 1969 at age 22 and completed PhD at Cambridge in 1972 at age 25, but Nobel Prize-winning multiscale modeling work was published in 1975-1976 at age 28-29; no exceptional material milestone by age 26.
family_context_summary: Born in Pretoria, South Africa to a Jewish family from Lithuania; parents separated when he was 9; mother became a school teacher; aunt and uncle Max Sterne and Tikvah Alper were prominent scientists who hosted him in England.
parent_family_domain_summary: Levitt's aunt and uncle were prominent scientists: Max Sterne created an anthrax vaccine and Tikvah Alper discovered the prion, providing early exposure to scientific thinking and connections to the Cambridge scientific community.

name: Ichirou Mizuki
milestone_by_age_26: Released debut single 'Kimi ni sasageru Boku no Uta' on Nippon Columbia in 1968 at age 20, and by 1972 at age 24 recorded the iconic theme song for Mazinger Z, establishing himself as a pioneer of the anison (anime song) genre.
early_history_summary: Born Toshio Hayakawa in Setagaya, Tokyo, Mizuki loved singing from age 5 and decided to become a singer early. At 16 he won a singing contest at a major jazz club, giving him the opportunity to perform American pop songs onstage. He signed with Nippon Columbia and released his first single in 1968 at age 20, then pivoted to anime theme songs in 1971 with 'Genshi Shōnen Ryū ga Yoku,' followed by Mazinger Z in 1972.
family_context_summary: Born in Setagaya, Tokyo; grew up listening to jazz and standard vocal artists; decided to become a singer at age 5; family financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Tokyo entertainment hub, early singing, jazz club performance, anime boom, Nippon Columbia
evidence_summary: Ichirou Mizuki was born in Setagaya, Tokyo, and developed a passion for singing from age 5, growing up listening to jazz and standard vocal artists. At 16 he won a singing contest at a jazz club, gaining early live performance experience with American pop songs. He signed with Nippon Columbia and released his debut single at 20, then pivoted to anime theme songs in 1971, riding the wave of the booming anime and tokusatsu industry. His early advantages were limited to his Tokyo location at the center of Japan's entertainment industry and his self-driven early immersion in singing. Family background and financial support are not documented in reviewed sources.
